item.title: Ġabra Dictionary Update: Offline Maltese Lookup on Phones, Windows, and Linux
item.description:
Ġabra Maltese Dictionary now has an MDX edition for compatible readers on phones and computers. Mac users can continue using the native dictionary with macOS lookup features.

The earlier article introduced the Mac edition. The project has since moved from gabra-maltese-macos-dictionary to gabra-maltese-dictionary, adding ready-made MDX files and cross-platform conversion tools. You can download the dictionary for a phone without first converting it on a Mac.

Choose the format before downloading

The v1.0 release now contains both an MDX ZIP and the native macOS DMG. Their lookup coverage differs.

Edition Contents and lookup How to use it
MDX + CSS 19,831 searchable headwords containing 21,083 source records Import into an MDX-compatible reader
macOS .dictionary 21,083 entries with approximately 4.5 million searchable word forms Install in Dictionary and use supported system lookup features

The MDX headword count is lower because one headword can contain several records. The project’s validation report records all 21,083 source entries as retained. A lower headword count does not by itself mean entries were dropped.

The approximately 4.5 million searchable forms belong to the native macOS edition. MDX provides headword lookup without the same inflected-form index. Keep the native edition on Mac if you often look up conjugations or plurals while reading. MDX makes the entries portable, with a different search scope.

Continue using the native Mac dictionary

Download GabraMalteseDict_v1.0.dmg from Releases, open it, and copy Gabra.dictionary into ~/Library/Dictionaries. In Finder, press Shift-Command-G and enter that path if the folder is difficult to locate.

Open Dictionary, enable Ġabra Maltese Dictionary in Dictionary → Settings, and try a Maltese word. The native view displays definitions and any part-of-speech, phonetic, and root information present in the entry (see Figure 1).

Figure 1: The native macOS dictionary. Other platforms use the MDX edition described below.

In supported apps, use the Look Up contextual-menu command, three-finger tap, or Force Click. Choose the gesture in System Settings → Trackpad → Point & Click → Look up & data detectors. Spotlight dictionary results depend on your macOS configuration. Confirm lookup in Dictionary first, then check the other entry points.

You can keep an existing native installation. Adding the MDX edition does not require removing the Mac dictionary.

Import MDX on a phone or another computer

Download GabraMalteseDict_MDX_v1.0.zip. Extract these two files and keep them together:

1
2

Gabra.mdx
Gabra.css

Gabra.mdx contains the dictionary; Gabra.css controls entry styling. A reader may use its own default appearance when the stylesheet is missing, so transfer both files when copying or syncing the dictionary.

You also need an MDX-compatible reader. The ZIP supplies dictionary files, without installing a reader. The project README lists these choices:

Platform Readers listed by the project
iPhone / iPad OpenMDict or MDict
Android DictTango or MDict
Windows GoldenDict-ng or DictTango Windows
Linux GoldenDict-ng
MDX on macOS GoldenDict-ng or MDict; Apple Dictionary uses the native edition above

Use the reader’s dictionary-import or add-folder feature. On a phone or tablet, transfer both files into storage the reader can access. Import screens vary, so follow the selected app’s instructions.

Try a headword after importing and check its definition and appearance. Entries retain available parts of speech, phonetics, and roots. The stylesheet follows the reader’s light or dark theme; edit Gabra.css to customize it. Check a few entries because rendering can differ between readers.

If a word does not appear after importing

First check whether Ġabra appears in the reader’s dictionary list and is enabled. If it is missing, return to the import step and select the extracted Gabra.mdx, rather than the downloaded ZIP. For a desktop reader that scans folders, confirm that the configured folder contains the dictionary file.

If the dictionary is listed but a search returns nothing, open a known headword within the dictionary and try searching for it. This helps distinguish a loading problem from an unmatched query. A form copied from a sentence may be a conjugation or a plural. Try its dictionary form next. The native Mac edition has broader word-form lookup; changing MDX readers does not supply that missing index.

If definitions appear but the layout looks wrong, check that Gabra.css was transferred alongside the MDX. Keep the filenames unchanged. If the files ended up in different folders, put them together again and refresh or reimport them as your reader requires. Open several entries in dark mode too, checking that the text remains readable against the background.

Before relying on the dictionary somewhere without internet access, disconnect and look up a word. This checks that the files are actually available on the device, rather than waiting to download from cloud storage when you need them.

Rebuilding uses two separate tools

Download the ready-made files if you only want to use the dictionary. To customize the stylesheet or rebuild MDX, run these commands from the new repository’s root:

1
2
3
4

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python scripts/convert_to_mdx.py sources/gabra/Body.data

This requires Python 3.10 or newer and works on macOS, Windows, and Linux. On Windows, activate with .venv\Scripts\activate. Output goes into dictionaries/mdx/ as Gabra.mdx and Gabra.css. Edit assets/mdx/Gabra.css before building to change the generated stylesheet.

The included Body.data snapshot contains entry bodies extracted from an existing native dictionary. Rebuilding MDX from it does not fetch newer upstream data or regenerate the native word-form index. A newer build date alone does not indicate newer dictionary content.

The native edition has a separate BSON build, requiring macOS and Apple’s Dictionary Development Kit. Put one upstream .tar.gz containing gabra/lexemes.bson and gabra/wordforms.bson in data/, then run:

1

bash scripts/update_macos.sh

The result is macos/objects/Gabra.dictionary. Use bash scripts/update_macos.sh --install to install it too; an existing installed dictionary is backed up under build/ first. This script expects you to supply the upstream archive. It does not download the latest BSON automatically.

Data and licensing

Dictionary data comes from Ġabra / MLRS at the University of Malta under CC BY 3.0. Project code is licensed under GNU GPL v3. Check the data and code licenses separately when redistributing files or building another dictionary; the attribution page records the source.

Use the native edition for system integration and inflected-form lookup on Mac. Use MDX for headword lookup on other devices, keeping its stylesheet with the dictionary. Current downloads and build requirements are in the new repository README.

item.title: Convert MDX Dictionaries to macOS Dictionary with an Agent Skill
item.description:
This post introduces MDX to macOS Dictionary, an open-source Agent Skill that turns local MDict .mdx dictionaries into searchable native macOS .dictionary bundles and ready-to-install DMG files.

MDX is a popular format for dictionary data, but macOS Dictionary.app cannot use an .mdx file directly. Converting one usually means preparing XML, compiling it with Apple’s Dictionary Development Kit, preserving styles, and packaging the result. This skill brings those steps into one guided workflow.

What the skill creates

Give a supported coding agent a local .mdx file or dictionary folder, and the skill can:

  • extract the dictionary entries from MDX;
  • convert them into Apple’s searchable dictionary format;
  • preserve companion CSS when it is available;
  • use a supplied cover or logo as the dictionary icon;
  • build a drag-to-install DMG installer;
  • install the finished dictionary in ~/Library/Dictionaries/ when requested.

The original MDX, CSS, JavaScript, and MDD files are left untouched. The result is a native dictionary that can be enabled in Dictionary.app and used from macOS features such as Spotlight and Look Up.

Why convert an MDX dictionary?

An MDX dictionary is convenient to share between compatible dictionary applications, but it is separate from the dictionary service built into macOS. A native .dictionary bundle fits more naturally into the Mac:

  • search entries from Dictionary.app;
  • use macOS’s Look Up feature on selected text;
  • access the dictionary from Spotlight where supported;
  • keep several dictionaries together in the system’s own dictionary folder;
  • install the result from a familiar DMG window.

This is useful for language learners, researchers, translators, and anyone who already owns a useful MDX dictionary and wants it to feel like part of macOS.

Install the Agent Skill

The skill is available on GitHub:

Jingyuan-Zheng/mdx-to-macos-dictionary-skill

If you use a compatible coding agent, install it with:

1

npx skills add Jingyuan-Zheng/mdx-to-macos-dictionary-skill --agent codex

After installation, ask the agent to convert a local .mdx file or folder. The skill checks the Mac’s prerequisites first and explains what needs attention before starting the conversion.

What the conversion looks like

The workflow is designed to keep the complicated parts together:

  1. Select a local MDX dictionary and any companion CSS, JS, MDD, cover, or logo files.
  2. Let the skill check the required macOS tools.
  3. It extracts the entries and builds the native Apple Dictionary data.
  4. It verifies the finished .dictionary bundle and creates a DMG installer.
  5. The dictionary can then be copied into the user’s Dictionary folder and enabled in Dictionary.app.

You can request an output-only conversion if you do not want the skill to install anything. Otherwise, it installs the completed bundle in the current user’s ~/Library/Dictionaries/ folder. An existing dictionary with the same name is not replaced without approval.

What you need on the Mac

The project runs on macOS and uses Apple’s dictionary-building tools. Depending on the Mac and the source dictionary, it may require:

  • Python 3;
  • Xcode Command Line Tools;
  • Rosetta on Apple Silicon Macs;
  • Homebrew’s create-dmg tool.

The skill checks these requirements before processing a dictionary. It can also obtain the open-source components it needs, including mdict-utils, Apple’s Dictionary Development Kit, and DMG Maker, while keeping the conversion work inside a separate working directory.

From a finished dictionary to everyday use

After installation, open Dictionary.app, choose Dictionary → Settings (or Dictionary → Preferences on older macOS versions), and enable the new dictionary. You can change its position in the list to control which source appears first.

Once enabled, select a word in a supported Mac app and use Look Up, or open Dictionary.app and search normally. With a compatible trackpad, you can also tap the selected word with three fingers. On a Force Touch trackpad, you can press firmly instead, using Force Click. These gestures use the Look Up & data detectors option in System Settings → Trackpad; the available choice depends on your Mac and macOS version. Apple documents the gesture options in Look up words on Mac.

Two open-source dictionaries from my projects

This Skill is meant to make projects like these easier to package and share. I have already written about two Mac dictionaries built from open dictionary data:

  • The Little Dict Mac 版 — a large English dictionary converted from MDX into Apple’s native .dictionary format, with support for Dictionary.app and trackpad Look Up.
  • Ġabra Maltese Dictionary for macOS — an open-source Maltese dictionary with millions of inflected forms, packaged for Dictionary.app, Spotlight, and three-finger or Force Click Look Up.

They show the practical result of the conversion workflow: a dictionary is no longer just a file to open in a separate reader, but a source that can participate in the Mac’s built-in lookup experience.

How it works

The skill uses mdict-utils to read the MDX entries, converts them to the XML structure expected by Apple’s Dictionary Development Kit, and compiles that data into a .dictionary bundle. It validates the generated XML and checks that the bundle contains the indexes, metadata, stylesheet, and dictionary body before packaging it.

The project is MIT licensed and available on GitHub. For the DMG packaging step itself, see DMG Maker.
